segments.say: Lesson 9. rag: The Full Pipeline. Ingest leads to chunk leads to embed leads to store leads to retrieve leads to augment leads to generate, with every stage animated.

rag (retrieval-augmented generation) means: before the L L M answers, search your own documents for the relevant pieces and paste them into the prompt, so the answer is grounded in your data. Here is an analogy. An open-book exam. The model is a smart student who hasn't read your company wiki; rag is the librarian who hands over the right 4 pages just before each question.

Why does this matter? The most common L L M application in companies: chat over docs, support bots, internal search. Directly relevant for GenAI / rag engineering roles. A few key words. Retrieval: Finding the relevant chunks for a question. Augmentation: Adding those chunks to the prompt. Chunk: A small piece of a document (a few paragraphs). Grounded: Based on provided sources, with citations. Vector database: Stores embeddings for fast similarity search.

segments.say: Now the model answers from the provided text and can cite the source. No retraining was needed. Update the doc and the next answer is up to date.
Offline: indexing pipeline. Sources: your private knowledge such as runbooks, wikis, P D Fs and past incidents. The L L M has never seen this data.
Load & clean: parse each format (P D F, H T M L, tables), strip headers and footers, keep useful metadata (source, date, team, access level).
Chunk: split into retrievable pieces with a little overlap so ideas aren't cut mid-thought.
Embed: each chunk becomes a vector.
Store: vectors plus original text plus metadata go into a vector index (pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, F A I S S. ).
Online: answering a question. A user asks a question the base model can't answer from training data.
Embed the question with the same embedding model used for the chunks.
Retrieve: approximate nearest-neighbour search finds the closest chunk vectors. Metadata filters (team, date, permissions) can narrow the search.
Return the top-k chunks (for example 4) with their sources.
Augment: build the prompt: instructions plus retrieved context in delimiters plus the question plus "answer only from the context, cite sources".
Generate: the L L M reads the context and writes the answer.
A grounded answer with citations, no fine-tuning needed. Update a doc and you just re-index it.

Why rag exists. L L Ms don't know your private or recent data (training cutoff). They hallucinate confidently. Grounding in retrieved text plus citations reduces that and makes answers verifiable. Cheaper and faster to update than fine-tuning: change a document, re-embed that chunk, done. Supports access control: filter retrieval by the user's permissions.

Where rag fails (and interviewers probe). Retrieval miss: the right chunk wasn't in the top-k. This is the most common failure, so fix retrieval before blaming the L L M. Bad chunking: the answer was split across chunks, or tables got mangled. Noisy context: irrelevant chunks distract the model. Unfaithful generation: the model ignores the context or adds facts. Stale index: docs changed but weren't re-indexed.
Analogy. An open-book exam. The L L M is a smart student; rag is the librarian who hands over the 4 most relevant pages just before each question.

Say it in the interview. "rag has an offline indexing path (load, clean, chunk, embed and store with metadata) and an online path (embed the query, retrieve top-k with metadata filters, optionally rerank, then generate with a grounded prompt that requires citations). When quality drops I debug retrieval first, using recall@k and context precision, before touching the prompt or the model.".

rag versus alternatives. Prompt only: only what fits in the prompt, manual, free, small, static context. rag: large private corpora, re-index docs, cheap, Q&A over docs, support, runbooks. Fine-tuning: weakly; mainly style and format, retrain, expensive, tone, format, domain behaviour. Long-context stuffing: if it fits, per request, high token cost, one-off analysis of a few docs.

A likely interview question: Walk me through a rag pipeline. A strong answer: Offline: load, clean, chunk, embed and store with metadata. Online: embed the query, filter and retrieve top-k, optionally rerank, build a grounded prompt, generate with citations. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
That's it for rag: The Full Pipeline. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
